title: Parametric vs non-parametric tests, and the key non-parametric tests
summary: The side-by-side comparison of parametric and non-parametric tests, why and when to use non-parametric tests, and the four key non-parametric tests with their business applications.

chunks.heading: Parametric vs non-parametric: the comparison table
chunks.explanation_md:
Learn this table row by row:

| Basis | Parametric tests | Non-parametric tests |
|---|---|---|
| Data type | Interval or ratio (continuous) | Ordinal or nominal |
| Distribution | Assumes normality | No assumption of distribution |
| Measure | Mean and SD | Medians and ranks |
| Example tests | t-test, ANOVA, regression | Chi-square, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis |
| Sample size | Usually large | Works with small samples |
| Use when | Data is symmetric, continuous | Data is skewed or categorical |
chunks.exam_line: Parametric: interval/ratio data, assumes normality, uses mean and SD, large samples (t-test, ANOVA, regression). Non-parametric: ordinal/nominal, no distribution assumption, medians and ranks, small samples (chi-square, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis).

chunks.heading: Why use non-parametric tests
chunks.exam_line: Use non-parametric tests when assumptions (normality, homogeneity) fail, data is ordinal or categorical, or small samples or outliers distort means; useful in Six Sigma, quality control, customer satisfaction and surveys.

chunks.heading: Four key non-parametric tests
chunks.explanation_md:
| Test | Type | Used when | Business application |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chi-square** | Categorical | Compare **observed vs expected frequencies** | Market share, preference counts |
| **Wilcoxon Signed-Rank** | Dependent (paired) | Compare **medians of matched data** | Pre/post customer feedback |
| **Mann-Whitney U** | Independent | Test differences between **two independent groups** | Compare supplier ratings |
| **Kruskal-Wallis** | Multiple groups | Compare **3+ independent groups** | Customer satisfaction across regions |

A useful way to hold these in your head: Wilcoxon is the paired case, Mann-Whitney U is the two-independent-groups case, and Kruskal-Wallis is the three-or-more-groups case.
chunks.exam_line: Chi-square: observed vs expected frequencies; Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: paired medians; Mann-Whitney U: two independent groups; Kruskal-Wallis: 3+ independent groups.

flashcards.front: Parametric vs non-parametric: sample size and use
flashcards.back: Parametric: usually large samples, symmetric continuous data. Non-parametric: works with small samples, skewed or categorical data.
Assumptions not met; ordinal or categorical data; small samples or outliers distort means. Useful in Six Sigma, quality control, customer satisfaction, surveys.
Categorical; compares observed vs expected frequencies; e.g. market share, preference counts.
Dependent (paired); compares medians of matched data; e.g. pre/post customer feedback.
Independent; tests differences between two independent groups; e.g. compare supplier ratings.
Multiple groups; compares 3+ independent groups; e.g. customer satisfaction across regions.
